title: Given strings s and t, count the number of distinct subsequences of s that equal t.
shortTitle: Distinct Subsequences — count occurrences of t as a subsequence of s

s1_definition.profdef: 2D counting DP where dp[i][j] is the number of ways the first i characters of s form the first j characters of t. If s[i−1]==t[j−1], dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] (use it) + dp[i−1][j] (skip it); otherwise dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j]. Base dp[i][0]=1. Time O(m·n), space O(n).
s1_definition.analogy: A pattern-counter at National Bank of India counts how many times a short approval code appears as an ordered (not necessarily contiguous) subsequence inside a long audit log. At each log character that matches the next needed code character, she either uses it or skips it, adding both counts.
s1_definition.oneliner: Match ⇒ use+skip (diagonal+above); mismatch ⇒ skip only (above). dp[i][0]=1.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 2D counting DP where dp[i][j] is the number of ways the first i characters of s form the first j characters of t. If s[i−1]==t[j−1], dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] (use it) + dp[i−1][j] (skip it); otherwise dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j]. Base dp[i][0]=1. Time O(m·n), space O(n).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A pattern-counter at National Bank of India counts how many times a short approval code appears as an ordered (not necessarily contiguous) subsequence inside a long audit log. At each log character that matches the next needed code character, she either uses it or skips it, adding both counts.

**One line to remember:** Match ⇒ use+skip (diagonal+above); mismatch ⇒ skip only (above). dp[i][0]=1.

sections.s2_technical:
Build a table dp of size (m+1) by (n+1). The first column dp[i][0] is one, because the empty target t is always matchable exactly once by taking no characters. The first row (except the corner) is zero, because a non-empty target cannot be formed from an empty s.

When s at i−1 equals t at j−1, the current s character may be used to match the current t character, contributing dp[i−1][j−1], or skipped, contributing dp[i−1][j], so dp[i][j] is their sum. For example: `if (s.charAt(i-1)==t.charAt(j-1)) dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]+dp[i-1][j]; else dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j];`. When they differ, the s character cannot help, so we only carry the skip count. The answer is dp[m][n].

The time is O(m·n), space reduces to O(n) by iterating j from high to low on a single row. A senior nuance is that counts can grow very large (they commonly overflow int on big inputs), so production code uses long or modular arithmetic.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, an audit tool counts how many times a short approval code appears as an ordered subsequence within a long transaction log, to gauge how many potential approval chains exist. This is exactly how Distinct Subsequences works.

Problem 2 — Each matching log character offers a choice to use or skip it, and all choices must be counted. This is exactly why the match case sums the use and skip subproblems.

The mini-project builds a `SubsequenceCounter`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input strings are rabbbit for s and rabbit for t.

Step 1: The first column is all ones because the empty target is matched once by taking nothing.

Step 2: The r, a, b characters line up and start building counts along matching diagonals.

Step 3: The three consecutive b characters in rabbbit create multiple ways to choose two b characters for rabbit, each adding the use and skip subproblems.

Step 4: The remaining i and t characters match and carry the accumulated counts.

Step 5: The bottom-right cell holds three, and babgbag containing bag yields five.

```text
2026-10-27T04:20:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Approval Audit (Distinct Subsequences)
2026-10-27T04:20:00Z [INFO] Distinct subsequence count = 3
2026-10-27T04:20:00Z [INFO] rabbbit contains rabbit → 3
2026-10-27T04:20:00Z [INFO] Distinct subsequence count = 5
2026-10-27T04:20:00Z [INFO] babgbag contains bag → 5
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  s=rabbbit  t=rabbit
  dp[i][0]=1 (empty target)
  match ⇒ dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1] + dp[i-1][j]   (use + skip)
  mismatch ⇒ dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j]               (skip only)
  dp[m][n] = 3   (three ways to pick "rabbit")
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Distinct Subsequences is a two-dimensional counting dynamic programming problem. I define dp of i and j as the number of ways the first i characters of the source string can form the first j characters of the target. The base case is the entire first column being one, because the empty target is always matched exactly once by taking no characters.

The transition depends on whether the current source character matches the current target character. When they match I have a choice: use the source character to satisfy the target character, which contributes the diagonal cell, or skip the source character, which contributes the cell above, so I add both. When they differ the source character cannot help, so I carry only the skip count from the cell above. The answer is the bottom-right cell.

In my project at National Bank of India, an audit tool counted how many times a short approval code appeared as an ordered subsequence within a long transaction log, to gauge how many potential approval chains existed. Because each matching character offered a use-or-skip choice, I summed those two subproblems, and I used long types because these counts can easily overflow a thirty-two-bit integer on large logs.
